content.content:
2270:\subsection{Overloading with static parameters}
\subsection{Overloading with static parameters}
\seclabel{revival-overloading}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{overloading-terms};
\secref{functional-applicability}; \secref{dotted-method-applicability};
\secref{resolving-overloading}; \secref{principles-overloading};
\secref{overloading-static-params}; \secref{resolving-coercion}; and, in a
draft build, the proposed features of the appendix ``Internal Document''.
\item[Change] The sentence of \secref{overloading-terms} that declarations of
one name may not differ in their static parameters, and its echo in
\secref{principles-overloading}, are replaced: declarations of one name may have
different static parameters, or some of them static parameters and others none,
and a declaration with static parameters is read as one declaration whose
parameter type ranges over its instances.
Such a declaration is applicable to a call when some instance of it within its
bounds is, and it is compared with others on the parameter types they declare,
taken over all their instances; the static arguments that a call does not write
are inferred for the declaration it selects, after the selection
(\chapref{type-inference}).
The three sentences of \chapref{multiple-dispatch} that inferred static
parameters before applicability was checked and before declarations were
compared, and the chapter's assumption that the static variables of a call have
been instantiated or inferred, are rewritten to match.
A new section, \secref{overloading-static-params}, states for declarations with
static parameters the three rules of the type group's paper of 2011, the No
Duplicates Rule, the Meet Rule and the Return Type Rule, the last checked over
every instance of the less specific declaration; how two parameter types with
static parameters exclude each other, by existential reduction with
instantiation exclusion; and a pair that the Return Type Rule refuses, in the
shape of that paper's own example, beside the pair that repairs it.
A box in that section states the restriction that the compiled implementation
adds, that of two declarations with as many static parameters of their own, one
of which is more specific than the other, the two agree on their static
parameters position by position, with an override that reorders them as its
example.
A later revision states the section's No Duplicates Rule on the relation without
``and not the other way round'', that $d_1$ and $d_2$ are not each applicable to
every call to which the other is applicable, with a box.
\secref{resolving-coercion} says in three places that a declaration with static
parameters is applicable when some instance of it is, that it is compared on the
parameter types it declares, and that the declaration selected is then
instantiated, the coercions of its instance inserted statically.
In the internal document, the proposed features on relaxing the restrictions on
the static parameters of overloaded functionals and on overloading with static
parameters are marked done, Jan's example answered by \library's factory and the
questions on exclusion by the existential reduction.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival decided
on 26~September 2026 that the sentence goes and that this working draft states
the model of the type group's paper of 2011 (Allen, Hilburn, Kilpatrick,
Luchangco, Ryu, Chase, and Steele, ``Type Checking Modular Multiple Dispatch
with Parametric Polymorphism and Multiple Inheritance'', OOPSLA 2011;
\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/rules.tick}, lines 132--180, and
\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/setup.tick}, lines 393--397, in the revival's
repository), which the compiled type checker applies, with two changes to the
checker: the Return Type Rule checked over every instance, and the positional
restriction.
On 28~September 2026 it decided that a coercion makes a call possible and never
changes which declaration runs when one is applicable without it, declarations
being chosen on the parameter types they declare and the declaration chosen
being then instantiated.
Neither implementation enforced the sentence: the interpreter has overloaded
declarations with different static parameters since May 2007, the compiled type
checker applies the rules of that paper to them, and \library\ overload across
different static parameters throughout.
The sentence is text of 2009.
The Fortress~1.0 release of 2008 compared generic declarations instead by
using ``their bounds as their supertypes'', in a section whose type relations
``may be replaced when the static type checker and the type inference engine
are implemented'' (\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress.1.0.pdf},
Section~15.6.1), and the team's unfinished restart of this specification in
2012 dropped the sentence
(\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/overloading.tick},
lines 100--114, in the revival's repository).
The restart's Types chapter (Luchangco, 2012) gives function types that hold
generic and plain declarations together, as sets of arrow types and universal
arrow types, and drops from a quantified type a static parameter that appears
in none of its types
(\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick}, lines
553--558, 764--767 and 794--801).
The positional restriction is the compiled implementation's and not the
language's: its code generator hands the static arguments that a call writes,
by position, to whichever declaration dispatch reaches (row~398 of the
revival's gap ledger), while the type group's paper of 2019 instantiates a
dispatched declaration by substitution and renames static parameters freely
(Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, ``Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with
Variance'', POPL 2019, Sections~4 and~5.2).
That paper's soundness proof excludes an upper bound that names a type
parameter, its own included, and closed types, so that \library's families over a type parameter
bounded by an instance of a trait at itself, such as \STR{SUM}, \STR{BIG~MAX}
and those over \TYP{Integral}, rest on the rules of 2011 as the compiled type
checker implements them, and not on the proof of 2019.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md}
in the revival's repository.
The No Duplicates Rule was first stated on the strict sense of more specific
that the section defines, under which no two declarations are each more
specific than the other, so that it refused no pair, and two declarations each
applicable to every call to which the other is fell to the Meet Rule (row~696
of the revival's gap ledger).
The paper of 2011 defines its relation of specificity without strictness, one
declaration being more specific than another when every type to which the first
is applicable is one to which the second is, and its No Duplicates Rule
``forbids distinct declarations from being equally specific''
(\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/rules.tick}, lines 97--108, 158--162 and 184--185);
the paper of 2019 states it as ``Distinct method declarations must have
different applicable sets'' (Section~2.2), and its rules [No-Dup-Not-Less] and
[No-Dup-Not-Gtr] refuse exactly a pair whose domain types are each a subtype of
the other (Section~4.1 and Figure~5).
The restatement follows the revival's decision of 23~September 2026 that the
type group's later word, that paper among it, outweighs the early text; its
reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-popl-examples/REPORT.md} in the
revival's repository.
\item[Effect] Declarations of one name may differ in their static parameters,
as \library's do.
The compiled type checker refuses the pair of the Return Type Rule's example,
which it accepted before and whose compiled class then failed verification, and
an override whose return type reorders its static parameters, which it accepted
before and which then failed at run time (row~398).
Neither implementation runs every set these rules allow.
The compiled type checker refuses more than the Return Type Rule where the more
specific declaration's parameter type is an object type, as in
\EXP{\VAR{ident}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T} beside
\EXP{\VAR{ident}(x\COLON \TYP{Circle})\COLON \TYP{Circle}} where \TYP{Circle} is an
object (row~542); the compiled code generator fails on two declarations with
static parameters whose bounds differ, the pair the Return Type Rule allows in
\secref{overloading-static-params} among them, and on the example of the type
group's paper of 2019 that overloads a method over an array list and a list
(row~537); and the interpreter refuses at load two declarations with static
parameters of which no pair of parameter types excludes each other (row~159),
that example among them (row~539).
Jan's example is still not a valid overloading, its two declarations having the
same parameter type.
The compiled type checker applies the No Duplicates Rule as it is now stated:
it refuses two declarations whose parameter types, read over their instances,
are each a subtype of the other, ``There are multiple declarations of \VAR{dup}
with the same parameter type'', and the interpreter loads such a pair and runs
one of them (row~373).
The calculus of \appref{overloading-calculus} keeps its rule that two
declarations with the same number of parameters have static parameters with the
same bounds; it admits fewer overloadings than these chapters, so that its valid
programs are still valid, and its rules and its soundness claim are unchanged
(\secref{revival-calculi}).
\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/overloading.tex},
lines 100--108:
\begin{quote}
Although there may be multiple declarations with the same functional name,
it is an error for their static parameters to differ (up to
$\alpha$-equivalence), or for one declaration to have static parameters and
another to not have them.
Hence, static parameters do not enter into the determination of which
declarations are applicable, so we ignore them for most of this chapter.
\end{quote}
lines 137--138:
\begin{quote}
We assume throughout this chapter that all static variables in functional calls
have been instantiated or inferred.
\end{quote}
lines 173--175, and in the same words for the types $\Ps_0$ and $\Ps$ of a
dotted method declaration, lines 205--207:
\begin{quote}
If the parameter type $\Ps$ includes static parameters, they are inferred as
described in \chapref{type-inference} before checking the applicability of the
declaration to the call.
\end{quote}
lines 292--295:
\begin{quote}
If the declarations include static parameters, they are inferred as described
in \chapref{type-inference} before comparing their parameter types to determine
which declaration is more specific.
\end{quote}
and \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced/overloading.tex}, lines
95--103:
\begin{quote}
Overloaded declarations must have static parameters that are identical (up to
$\alpha$-equivalence).  Also, valid overloadings for declarations that contain
keyword or varargs parameters are determined by analyzing the expansion of these
declarations as described in \secref{applicability-with-special-params}.
Therefore, static parameters, keyword parameters, and varargs parameters are
ignored in the remainder of this chapter.
\end{quote}
The sentences added to \secref{resolving-coercion}, after the Working Draft's
lines 455--459, 522--524 and 567--570 of
\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/conversions-coercions.tex}, and the new
section have no counterpart there.
The new section, the revival's text of 30~September 2026, stated:
\begin{quote}
The \emph{No Duplicates Rule}: $d_1$ and $d_2$ are not each more specific than
the other.
\end{quote}
\item[Route C] The same under route~C, except that the existential reduction
uses the rule of \secref{revival-routec} in place of instantiation exclusion;
the No Duplicates Rule does not depend on the rule on instantiations.
\end{description}

\item[Affected sections] \secref{type-param}; \secref{principles-overloading}.

usage: ledger.py [-h] COMMAND ...

The gap ledger's tool: it owns the ledger's format, reads its rows, and is
the only way to write them.

positional arguments:
  COMMAND

options:
  -h, --help  show this help message and exit

usage: ledger.py COMMAND [ARGS] [--root DIR] [--ledger FILE] [--history FILE]

  heads                      one tab-separated line per row: number, status,
                             class, the claim's first 150 characters, and the
                             paths the row cites in backticks
  sections                   each section that holds a row table: its row
                             count and title, tab-separated
  section TITLE              the heads of that section's rows
  show N [--short]           row N under its section and table header; with
                             --short, its status, class, claim and the notes'
                             first 300 characters
  find WORDS [--open] [--cites FILE[:LINE]] [--all]
                             one line per row that holds every word (whole
                             words, or a word's start with a trailing *):
                             number, status, class, the claim's start; --open
                             leaves out FIXED, DUPLICATE and RETIRED; --cites
                             keeps the rows citing FILE (at LINE) and prints
                             the lines they cite; at most 10 rows unless --all
  count                      the rows by status, kind and area; nothing stored
  add FILE --section TITLE   FILE holds one row line, its # cell `?` (or the
                             seven cells after it); numbers it max + 1 and
                             inserts it in that section's table in number
                             order
  note N TEXT                appends TEXT to row N's notes
  close N --commit HASH --test NAME [--note TEXT] [--claim C] [--class C]
        [--spec C] [--found-by C]
                             after the fix has landed: HASH must be in HEAD's
                             history and NAME a test under the test folders;
                             writes the one-line FIXED row (the claim's first
        write_text(p.ledger, led.text())
    print('row %d, in "%s"' % (num, sec.title))
    files = backtick_paths(line)
    kin = sorted({r.num for r in led.rows if r.num != num for f in files if cites(r.line, f)})
    if kin:
        print('rows that cite the same files: %s' % ', '.join(map(str, kin[:20])) + (' and %d more' % (len(kin) - 20) if len(kin) > 20 else ''))


def cmd_note(a, p):
    text = escape_pipes(one_line(a.text))
    if not text:
        raise LedgerError('note needs a TEXT')
    with Lock(p.lock):
        led = Ledger(p.ledger)
        r = led.one(a.n)
        if r.status_word in ('FIXED', 'DUPLICATE'):
            raise LedgerError('row %d is %s: a closed row is not edited; its full text is in the history file' % (r.num, r.status_word))
        cells = r.template_cells()
        cells[7] = (cells[7] + ' ' + text).strip()
        line = join_cells(cells)
        template_row(line, {x.num for x in led.rows}, p.root)
        replace_rows(p, led, [(r, line, 'note added')])
    print('row %d: note added (%d characters)' % (r.num, len(line)))


def cmd_close(a, p):
    root = p.root
    if git(root, 'rev-parse', '--verify', '--quiet', a.commit + '^{commit}').returncode != 0:
        raise LedgerError('%s is not a commit' % a.commit)
    if git(root, 'merge-base', '--is-ancestor', a.commit, 'HEAD').returncode != 0:

## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number order. A pipe inside a cell is written `\|`. (POSITIONS, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, section 4.)

- **#**: the row's number, the next free one when it is added; never reused, renumbered or given to another row. 148 is vacant.
- **claim**: at most 300 characters, whose first 150 name the defect or the capability: what fails or what holds, and where.
- **status**: exactly one word of seven, with no second status and nothing in brackets:
  - `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`: it works; it ran and its output is recorded.
  - `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`: the specification settles it and the reproducer confirms it. A row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, and its notes say which half is fixed.
  - `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`: the failure reproduces; the mechanisms tried are named and are not exhaustive.
  - `CONTESTED`: unsettled; the notes say why.
  - `RETIRED`: a source's claim falsified here, kept so that it is not derived again.
  - `FIXED`: closed by a landed commit (`ledger.py close`): the claim's first sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed HASH; full text: history, row N`.
  - `DUPLICATE`: a pointer (`ledger.py duplicate`), notes `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`.
- **class**: `kind (area)`; `—` only for `POSITIVE-VERIFIED` and `RETIRED`. The kind is one of `implementation gap`, `library gap vs spec`, `library bug`, `design limit`, `deliberate`, `typesetter`, `packaging`; the area one of `parser`, `walk`, `checker`, `codegen`, `runtime`, `library`, `prelude`, `specification`, `tests`, `tools`.
- **spec citation**: the `.tex` file and the section heading in quotes, as `basic/operators/juxtameaning.tex`, "Juxtaposition"; a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; `silent` where the specification does not say.
- **reproducer**: one test (its name, or its path under the test folders; an `XXX` test while it is an expected failure) or one probe path from the repository root, at most 200 characters; `none` when nothing in the tree reproduces it, with the command and its output, or the probe's old path, in the notes.
- **found by**: the stream that found it (`climb batch 8 rung I`, `run-c3`, `apl rung 2`), at most 60 characters; no date and no role.
- **notes / workaround**: at most 700 characters: `siblings: N, M` first if there are any; the mechanism, with file:line and the commit it was true at; the workaround; for a closed row, `fixed HASH`.

A path under `explorations/` that is no longer in the tree is read from history: `git show $(git log -1 --diff-filter=D --format=%h -- PATH)^:PATH`.

content.content:
\section{Overloading Resolution}
\seclabel{resolving-overloading}

\note{
Victor: Does this paragraph, other than the last sentence,
really belong in this section?}

To evaluate a given functional call,
it is necessary to determine which functional declaration
to dispatch to.
To do so,
we consider the declarations that are applicable to that call at run time.
If there is exactly one such declaration,
then the call dispatches to that declaration.
If there is no such declaration,
then the call is \emph{undefined}, which is a static error.
(However, see \secref{applicability-with-coercion}
for how coercion may add to the set of applicable declarations.)
If multiple declarations are applicable to the call at run time,
then we choose an arbitrary declaration among the declarations such that
no other applicable declaration is more specific than them.
A declaration with static parameters is applicable to a call at run time, as
to a static call, when some instance of it whose static arguments satisfy
their bounds is applicable to the call, so the declaration to which a call
dispatches may be one that the static call did not select.
A declaration that the static call selected runs at the instance inferred for
the call (\secref{static-arg-inference}); any other declaration runs at the
instance in which each type parameter is the intersection of the upper bounds
placed on it: its declared bound, \TYP{Any} if it has none
(\secref{type-param}), and the bounds that the dynamic types of the arguments
place on it through the parameter types and that the static type of the call
places on it through the return type.
Where the type parameter is a static argument of a parameterized trait in a
parameter type, as \VAR{X} is in \EXP{t\COLON\TYP{Tag}\llbracket{}X\rrbracket},
the value of the argument fixes it, since no value belongs to two
instantiations of one parameterized trait (\secref{trait-types}); where it is
the whole type of a parameter, the dynamic type of the argument is only a
lower bound, and the type parameter is its bound under the static type of the
call.
The type parameters of a declaration that only dispatch reaches are never
instantiated with \TYP{BottomType}, nor with the union of the types of the
arguments.
\revision{revival-dispatch}{The Working Draft of February 2011 did not say at
which instance a declaration with static parameters runs when dispatch reaches
it and the static call selected another.
The rule stated is the one by which the dispatcher of the type group's paper of
2019 instantiates a declaration (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, ``Polymorphic
Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with Variance'', POPL 2019); the team had assumed
the union of the lower bounds and could not prove it correct.
Both implementations of the revival take the dynamic type of the argument where
the value does not fix the type parameter: the interpreter because it has no
static types, and so no static type of the call to bound the instance, as with
its choice of coercions (\secref{resolving-coercion}); the compiled path because
its dispatcher reads the static arguments of a dispatched declaration from the
value and is not given the static type of the call.
Where the value fixes the type parameter, the two rules give the same instance.
The compiled path's departure is gated as an expected failure (row~538 of the
revival's gap ledger), and the compiled path does not yet run the second
example below (row~496).}

- F-146 **The compiled checker accepts arithmetic in a size and opens a value of a trait whose `comprises` clause lists a type at a `where`-clause size.** It builds P-55, with array fork 3 at its default. A name or an operation beside a numeral counts as not known to differ, and two different size parameters as different (row 683, contested). The checker opens each listed type's `nat` and `int` `where`-clause sizes as fresh names, and walk reads them as any size. Gated by `compiler_tests/NatArith*` and `NatOpenChecker`. Open: an opened size does not compile (row 307), walk stops on a power in a size (row 676), and rows 636, 675, 681 and 682 (contested). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-size-expressions/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 12.
- F-176 **The specification allows arithmetic in a size, and two size expressions are the same type when they are written alike once numerals are folded.** It states P-55. A size may be a numeral, a name, a sum, a difference, a product, a power to a numeral or a name, or a bracketed expression. A static parameter is not known to differ from a numeral. F-146 gives the compiled checker. Walk computes `+`, `-` and juxtaposition at instantiation, stops on a power (row 676), and binds only a name or a numeral at a call. Source: `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex:49-62`.

content.content:
\section{Principles of Overloading}
\seclabel{principles-overloading}

Fortress allows multiple functional declarations of the same name to
be declared in a single scope.  However, recall from \chapref{names}
the following shadowing rules:
\begin{itemize}
\item
dotted method declarations shadow top-level function declarations with
the same name, and
\item
dotted method declarations provided by a trait or object declaration
or object expression
shadow functional method declarations with the same name that are
provided by a different trait or object declaration
or object expression.
\end{itemize}

\section{Subtype Rule}
\seclabel{subtype-rule}

If the parameter type of one declaration is a subtype of the parameter
type of another (and they are not the same) then there is no
ambiguity between these two declarations: for every call to which both
are applicable, the first is more specific.  This is the basis of the
Subtype Rule.

The Subtype Rule also requires a relationship between the return types
of the two declarations.  Without such a requirement, a program may
violate type safety.

\paragraph{The Subtype Rule for Functions and Functional Methods:}

This section proves that the overloading rules for
function declarations are sufficient to guarantee no undefined nor
ambiguous call at run time (the case for methods is analogous).

The proof covers declarations whose parameter types and return types have no
static parameters, and calls to which declarations are applicable without
coercion.

rules, so that no two of them have the same parameter type; that each of them has

transitive; and that every value of a trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause is a
